title: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS THEY'RE ALREADY SAFE
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS THEY'RE ALREADY SAFE

What if the people we expect to see standing closest to Jesus are the very people who have misunderstood His heart? A shocking warning about pride, a scandalous story about grace, and the Kingdom where everything we thought made us important is turned upside down.
Not because He was threatening everyone who had faithfully followed Him.
Not because He wanted His disciples to live in fear.
But because He knew something terrifying about the human heart.
We can spend years doing things for God while quietly beginning to believe that God owes us something.
We can serve until our bodies are exhausted, give until our wallets feel empty, pray until our knees ache, and still carry a secret question we would never dare say aloud:
“Lord, after everything I've done for You… don't I deserve more than this?”
And then Jesus speaks words that dismantle the entire way we measure spiritual greatness.
“But many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.” — Matthew 19:30 (KJV)
Read that again.
The first will be last.
The last will be first.
Not necessarily the richest becoming poor or the poorest becoming rich. Not merely the famous becoming forgotten or the forgotten becoming famous.
Something much deeper is happening.
Jesus is exposing the dangerous difference between being impressive in the eyes of people and being humble before the heart of God.
And the most unsettling part?
He said these words while speaking to people who had sacrificed to follow Him.
People like Peter.
People who had left their livelihoods, their security, and their familiar lives behind.
People who were not pretending to be disciples.
They really were disciples.
Which means this warning is not something we can comfortably throw at unbelievers while congratulating ourselves for being Christians.
It reaches right into the church.
Right into the ministry.
Right into the worship team.
Right into the heart of the person reading this article.
And perhaps… right into yours.
To understand what Jesus meant, we have to return to the moment when a wealthy young man approached Him.
The man had everything society admired.
Possessions. Status. Religious discipline. A respectable reputation.
And yet, something was missing.
He approached Jesus asking what good thing he must do to have eternal life.
Jesus eventually confronted the attachment that ruled his heart, telling him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The young man walked away sorrowful.
Matthew tells us why.
He had great possessions.
But perhaps the more revealing truth is that his possessions had a great hold on him.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted the blessing of God.
He wanted the assurance that everything would be all right.
But when Jesus confronted the thing he could not bear to surrender, his feet carried him away from the very Savior he had approached.
Imagine that moment.
The dust beneath his sandals.
The silence after Jesus' words.
The disciples watching him disappear.
A man who appeared to possess everything walked away from the One who offered the life he could never purchase.
And Jesus turned to His disciples and taught them how difficult it is for the rich to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.
Not because wealth itself makes salvation impossible.
Not because every wealthy person is condemned.
But because riches can become a rival master, convincing the heart that it is secure, self-sufficient, and in control.
The disciples were astonished.
“Who then can be saved?” they asked.
Jesus answered with one of the most beautiful declarations in Scripture.
“With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.” — Matthew 19:26 (KJV)
There it is.
Before Jesus ever tells the parable of the workers in the vineyard, He establishes the foundation.
Salvation is not a human achievement.
It is a divine miracle.
No amount of wealth can buy it.
No record of religious activity can manufacture it.
No impressive spiritual résumé can force heaven's doors open.
What human beings cannot accomplish through their own power, God accomplishes through His grace.
But Peter had a question.
A deeply human question.
A question that sounds remarkably familiar when we are tired, disappointed, or secretly comparing our sacrifices with someone else's blessings.
“Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?” — Matthew 19:27 (KJV)
In other words:
“Lord, we stayed when that rich young man walked away.”
“We surrendered what he refused to surrender.”
“We left everything to follow You.”
“So what will we receive?”
Peter was not wrong to recognize that following Jesus involved sacrifice. Nor was Jesus offended by the idea that God rewards faithfulness.
In fact, Jesus answered Peter with remarkable promises.

He spoke of the future renewal, when the Son of Man would sit upon His glorious throne. He promised the apostles a significant role in that coming kingdom, and He assured those who sacrificed for His name that their surrender would not be forgotten.
Jesus does not despise faithful service.
He does not overlook hidden obedience.
He does not forget the sacrifices no one else sees.
But He also knows how quickly gratitude can turn into entitlement.
How easily obedience can become a transaction.
How subtly a servant can begin thinking like a creditor.
And so He adds the warning:
“The first shall be last; and the last shall be first.”
Then, in Matthew 20, Jesus tells a story that would have sounded almost offensive to people who believed reward must always be calculated according to visible effort.
A landowner goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
They agree to work for a denarius, a normal day's wage.
The workers begin at dawn.
The sun rises.
The hours stretch.
Their backs bend.
Their hands grow tired.
Dust clings to their skin.
They labor through the heat of the day.
Later, the landowner goes out again and hires more workers.
Then more.
And more.
Finally, near the eleventh hour, when the working day is almost finished, he finds others still standing idle.
“Why stand ye here all the day idle?” he asks.
They answer:
“Because no man hath hired us.” — Matthew 20:7 (KJV)
Don't rush past that sentence.
Because no one hired us.
Not necessarily because they were lazy.
Not necessarily because they refused to work.
The story does not tell us everything about their circumstances.
It simply reveals that, until that moment, nobody had brought them into the vineyard.
Can you imagine standing there as the day fades?
Watching other men chosen.
Watching other workers leave with purpose.
Watching the opportunities disappear.
Wondering whether your family would have enough to eat.
Wondering whether tomorrow would be any different.
Perhaps you know something about that feeling.
Being overlooked.
Being the last person considered.
Watching others receive opportunities you prayed for.
Watching someone younger advance while you remain stuck.
Watching people who seem less faithful enjoy blessings you have begged God to provide.
Or perhaps you know the deeper shame of believing you have arrived too late.
Too many wasted years.
Too many broken promises.
Too many nights you wish you could erase.
Too much damage done.
Too many chances squandered.
And somewhere inside, a voice whispers:
“God might forgive you, but you will never matter as much as the people who got everything right from the beginning.”
Then the landowner speaks.
“Go ye also into the vineyard.”
They are invited in.
Even at the eleventh hour.
Even when the day is nearly finished.
Even when everyone else seems to have had a head start.
And when evening comes, the landowner tells his steward to pay the workers, beginning with those who arrived last.
Then something astonishing happens.
The men who worked only one hour receive a full denarius.
The same amount promised to those who had labored since morning.
Imagine their faces.
The surprise.
The relief.
Perhaps the thought of returning home with enough to provide for their families.
They had expected so little.
Yet they received more than they had reason to anticipate.
But the workers who arrived first began doing calculations.
If those men received a denarius for one hour, surely we will receive more.
We carried the burden.
We endured the heat.
We were here when the vineyard was nearly empty.
We deserve more.
But when their turn came, they also received a denarius.
Exactly what had been promised.
And suddenly, what had been a fair agreement in the morning felt unfair in the evening.
Not because the landowner had taken anything from them.
But because he had been generous to someone else.
That is where Jesus' story becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes the blessing that exposes our hearts is not the blessing we failed to receive.
It is the blessing God gave someone else.
You prayed for years to see a family member come to Christ.
Someone else shares a testimony of an unexpected conversion, and instead of rejoicing, you feel a quiet bitterness.
You have served faithfully in the background.
Someone new receives public recognition, and suddenly your hidden obedience feels worthless.
You have walked with Jesus for decades.
A person with a scandalous past repents, finds forgiveness, and is warmly welcomed into the Christian community.
And something inside you whispers:
“After everything they did… why should they be celebrated?”
That whisper is dangerous.
Not because justice does not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because wrongdoing should be ignored.
But because envy can make us resent the mercy that rescued us.
The first workers complained.
The landowner answered:
“Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?” — Matthew 20:13 (KJV)
The word “penny” in this older English translation refers to a denarius, not a modern one-cent coin.
The landowner had kept his agreement.
Then he asked:
“Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — Matthew 20:15 (KJV)
In the original Greek, the final question reads:
ἢ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἀγαθός εἰμι;
A close translation is:
“Or is your eye evil because I am good?”
The phrase “evil eye” is an ancient idiom associated with envy, resentment, or a begrudging attitude.
Jesus is not talking about a supernatural curse cast through someone's eyes.
He is confronting a heart that looks upon generosity and responds with bitterness.
The landowner's goodness had become offensive to the workers who believed they deserved special treatment.
Think about that.
They were not angry because they received nothing.
They were angry because someone else received generosity.
And if we are willing to be painfully honest, there are moments when that same ugliness lives inside us.
We celebrate grace when it rescues us.
But sometimes we question grace when it reaches someone we think deserves less.
We rejoice when Jesus forgives our sins.
But we struggle when He forgives the person who hurt us.
We are thankful that God has been patient with our failures.
But we become impatient when He shows mercy to someone whose failures are more public.
We want grace to cover our history.
But we want strict accounting for theirs.
And Jesus confronts us with a question that cannot be answered through religious performance.
Have you begun to resent God's goodness because it refuses to follow your personal ranking system?
The Greek expression Jesus uses at the conclusion of the parable is equally important.
Οὕτως ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι.
“So the last will be first, and the first last.” — Matthew 20:16
The Greek words eschatoi and prōtoi mean “last” and “first.”
Jesus is describing a reversal of expected order.
He is challenging the assumption that human status, seniority, and visible achievement automatically determine one's place in God's Kingdom.
And notice the word “so.”
The conclusion is tied directly to the story.
The landowner's generosity exposes the workers' expectations.
The final payment reveals the difference between receiving a promised wage and demanding superiority over others.
The point is not that laziness is better than faithfulness.
It is not that someone should deliberately postpone repentance until the end of life.
It is not that every Christian will receive precisely the same heavenly responsibilities or rewards regardless of faithfulness.
Scripture teaches that God sees and evaluates our works. Paul speaks of believers' work being tested in 1 Corinthians 3:12–15, and Jesus repeatedly teaches the importance of faithful stewardship.
Nor should we treat this parable as a complete economic blueprint for earthly employment contracts.
Its central subject is the Kingdom of Heaven.
The point is that God's generosity cannot be reduced to the calculations of human entitlement.
His grace does not become unjust simply because it is more generous than someone expected.
His Kingdom does not operate according to our obsession with being more important than the next person.
And this truth becomes even more beautiful when we understand the larger biblical picture.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word חֵן (ḥēn) often carries the sense of favor or grace.
Genesis 6:8 says:
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression is:
וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
VeNoaḥ matza ḥēn be'enei Adonai — commonly expressed in English as, “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.”
The divine name is represented in the Hebrew text by the four letters יהוה, traditionally read as Adonai in Jewish liturgical practice.
This does not mean the Hebrew ḥēn and the Greek word for grace are identical in every usage.
But it does show that divine favor is not a New Testament invention.
God's gracious character runs throughout the biblical story.
And when we arrive at the New Testament, we encounter the Greek word:
χάρις (charis) — grace, favor, or gift, depending on context.
Paul writes:
Read those words slowly.
Not of yourselves.
The gift of God.
Not of works.
Lest any man should boast.
The cross leaves no room for spiritual arrogance.
No one will stand before Jesus and truthfully declare:
“I earned my salvation.”
No one will look at the wounds of the crucified Savior and say:
“My righteousness made Your sacrifice unnecessary.”
The Christian who has walked faithfully with God for sixty years and the repentant sinner who turns to Christ near the end of life must both depend on the same Savior.
Both need mercy.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need the righteousness that comes through Christ.
And neither has the right to boast as though salvation were a personal accomplishment.
This does not make sixty years of faithfulness meaningless.
Far from it.
Those years may be filled with the joy of knowing Christ, the fruit of obedience, the blessing of serving others, and the deepening transformation of the Holy Spirit.
But they do not turn salvation into a debt that God owes.
That distinction changes everything.
And perhaps no scene illustrates it more vividly than the crucifixion.
There, beside Jesus, hung a condemned criminal.
A man facing the consequences of his crimes.
A man with no remaining lifetime in which to build a respectable religious reputation.
No opportunity to spend decades serving in ministry.
No chance to demonstrate years of visible spiritual growth.
No impressive record of good works to present.
Only a dying body.
A guilty past.
And a desperate appeal.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
What could this man offer Jesus?
He could not climb down from the cross and repair every wrong he had committed.
He could not undo the damage of his past.
He could not promise fifty years of service.
He had nothing with which to bargain.
But he turned toward the crucified King in faith.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
Pause there.
Let the weight of that moment settle.
A condemned man, whose earthly story was almost over, received a promise from the Savior of the world.
Not because his crimes were insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because holiness did not matter.
But because Jesus Christ has authority to save those who turn to Him.
The criminal's faith was not an excuse for his wrongdoing.
It was a turning toward the only One who could save him.
And while the thief on the cross is not himself one of the workers in Matthew 20, his story beautifully illustrates a related truth:
The mercy of Christ is not reserved for people who had an early start.
Perhaps you are reading this with a history you cannot erase.
A marriage damaged by your choices.
Children who remember your anger.
Parents whose trust you betrayed.
Years lost to addiction.
Promises broken.
Secret sins.
A faith that once burned brightly but has become buried beneath disappointment.
Perhaps you are not proud of the person you have become.
Perhaps you avoid certain worship songs because they remind you of the person you used to be.
And maybe you have been telling yourself:
“I should have come back to God years ago.”
Maybe you should have.
But hear this carefully.
The fact that you should have returned yesterday is not a reason to refuse His call today.
The vineyard is not yours to control.
The mercy is not yours to purchase.
The Savior is not waiting for you to manufacture a perfect history before you approach Him.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
He does not promise that repentance erases every earthly consequence.
Some relationships require rebuilding.
Some wounds take years to heal.
Some wrongs demand confession, restitution, accountability, and a changed life.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying what God calls holy.
But grace means your past does not have to be the final authority over your future.
And that is why the Gospel is not merely inspiring.
It is scandalous.
Not scandalous because God ignores justice.
But because the One who is perfectly just has made a way to justify sinners through the saving work of His Son.
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Christ bore sin's judgment.
The innocent Savior suffered for the guilty.
As Peter writes:
The just for the unjust.
That is the heart of redemption.
Jesus did not come merely to rearrange the social rankings of religious people.
He came to save sinners, reconcile them to God, and create a people transformed by His grace.
And those who have received such mercy are called to become merciful themselves.
But there is another side to this teaching.
A side that should unsettle those of us who have been in church for years.
Because the first workers in Jesus' parable were not outsiders.
They were already inside the vineyard.
Already working.
Already participating.
Their problem was not that they refused to enter.
Their problem was the resentment that surfaced when generosity was shown to others.
It is possible to be active in religious service while becoming spiritually cold.
Possible to defend sound doctrine while speaking cruelly to wounded people.
Possible to give generously while secretly craving applause.
Possible to know Scripture while refusing to forgive.
Possible to preach humility while demanding special treatment.
Possible to celebrate testimonies publicly while privately resenting the attention someone else receives.
And yes, possible to build a ministry around the name of Jesus while slowly making the ministry's success more important than the Jesus it claims to serve.
That is a warning I believe every Christian leader, writer, preacher, and content creator must take seriously.
Including those of us serving through Gospel Warrior.
If people remember our name but never encounter the truth of Christ, we have missed the purpose.
If we gain followers but fail to make disciples, something essential has been lost.
If our words move people emotionally but never lead them toward repentance, grace, biblical truth, and obedience, emotion alone is not enough.
Jesus must remain the center.
Not our platform.
Not our numbers.
Not our reputation.
Not our ability to make people cry.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Because there is a terrible possibility that a person could appear first in the eyes of a religious crowd while being dangerously far from the humility of Christ.
And there is a beautiful possibility that someone the world barely notices may be living a life of profound faithfulness before God.
The elderly widow praying alone.
The exhausted father resisting temptation when no one would ever know.
The mother quietly teaching her children Scripture.
The young believer choosing honesty when dishonesty would be profitable.
The former addict walking away from old companions because following Jesus now matters more than belonging to the crowd.
The struggling Christian who falls, repents, seeks help, and keeps turning back to Christ.
The unknown servant who cleans the church after everyone else goes home.
Heaven sees what the world overlooks.
Jesus taught:
“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” — Matthew 20:27 (KJV)
And immediately after that, He pointed to Himself.
“Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Matthew 20:28 (KJV)
Do you see how the pieces come together?
The first and the last.
The vineyard workers.
The warning against entitlement.
The call to humble service.
The Son of Man giving His life as a ransom.
Jesus is not merely teaching us how to become last so we can secretly manipulate our way into first place.
That would turn humility into another strategy for self-promotion.
He is teaching us to abandon our obsession with superiority and follow the King who humbled Himself for our salvation.
Paul describes Christ's humility in Philippians 2.
Though Christ existed in the form of God, He did not use His divine status for selfish advantage. He took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
Then God highly exalted Him.
The way of Christ overturns the world's definition of greatness.
The world says, “Make them serve you.”
Jesus says, “Serve one another.”
The world says, “Protect your image at all costs.”
Jesus calls us to walk in truth.
The world says, “You are only valuable when you are ahead.”
Jesus reveals a Kingdom where the humble are honored and the proud are warned.
The world says, “Never let anyone forget what they did.”
Jesus commands forgiveness, without requiring us to deny wrongdoing or abandon wise boundaries.
The world says, “Your past is your identity.”
The Gospel announces that those who belong to Christ are made new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
That is not a promise that every consequence disappears overnight.
It is the declaration that union with Christ changes who we are and the direction of our lives.
And now I want to ask you something that may be uncomfortable.
When was the last time you genuinely rejoiced because God blessed someone who had not worked as long as you?
When was the last time you celebrated a repentant sinner without quietly reminding yourself how much better your own record looked?
When was the last time you served without hoping someone would notice?
When was the last time you thanked God simply for allowing you to belong to Him?
Not for a platform.
Not for a title.
Not for an audience.
Not for a promotion.
Not for a miracle.
Just for Him.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that we sometimes fail to receive the recognition we desire.
Perhaps it is that we become so consumed with recognition that we stop enjoying the grace we already have.
The first workers began the day with an agreement.
They ended it with resentment.
The last workers began with uncertainty.
They ended it with unexpected generosity.
And the same goodness that brought joy to one group exposed envy in the other.
That is what grace does.
It comforts the broken.
And it confronts the proud.
It lifts the repentant sinner.
And it dismantles the illusion that any of us can save ourselves.
It invites the weary to come to Christ.
And it warns the religious heart against turning faithfulness into superiority.
So when Jesus says the first will be last and the last first, do not reduce His words to a promise that every overlooked person will eventually become famous.
That is far too small.
Do not twist them into a claim that obedience is worthless.
That is unbiblical.
Do not use them to excuse delayed repentance.
Tomorrow is not promised.
And do not assume they mean God treats every act of faithfulness as though it has no significance.
He is a righteous Judge who sees everything.
Instead, hear the warning and the invitation together.
Stop measuring your worth by where you stand compared with someone else. Start measuring your life by whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
If you have followed Him for decades, remain grateful.
If you have just come to faith, remain humble.
If you are serving in obscurity, do not despise your calling.
If you have received responsibility and influence, do not mistake them for proof of spiritual superiority.
If you have wandered, repent and return.
If you are hiding sin, bring it into the light.
If you have wounded others, take responsibility.
If you have been wounded, seek the healing, truth, and wise support you need.
And if you have been looking at someone else's restoration with resentment, ask God to give you a heart that rejoices when mercy triumphs over a sinner's past.
Because the Kingdom of Heaven is not a competition to see which forgiven sinner can feel most superior.
It is a Kingdom ruled by the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And one day, when everything hidden is brought into the light, the applause of this world will not determine what matters.
Jesus will.
There is a prayer I hope you will carry away from this article.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for every moment I treated Your grace like something I had earned. Forgive me for comparing my journey with others. Forgive my pride, my envy, and my secret resentment. Teach me to rejoice when You restore the broken. Teach me to serve without demanding recognition. Give me a repentant heart, a humble spirit, and a love that reflects Yours. Keep me close to Your Word. And let my life glorify You, whether anyone notices me or not. Amen.”
If that prayer exposed something you have been carrying, please do not bury the conviction under another scroll.
You do not have to publish the details of your deepest wounds to ask for prayer.
Sometimes three honest words are enough to let another believer know you need encouragement.
This is also why I want to invite you to become part of what we are building through Gospel Warrior.
It doesn't.
Not because paying for ministry support counts as purchasing forgiveness, securing a blessing, or proving that you are a better Christian.
It doesn't.
And certainly not because anyone should feel guilty for being unable to give.
The Gospel is freely offered, and salvation is never for sale.
But when the Lord places a genuine desire in our hearts to help spread biblical truth, one practical expression of Christian generosity can be supporting trustworthy Gospel-centered work.
Scripture says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Paul's teaching emphasizes giving that is willing rather than reluctant or compelled.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
We encourage you to remain faithful to your local church and to give responsibly, prayerfully, and willingly.
These items are simply a practical expression of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
The reason is that people need the Gospel.
The person quietly questioning whether God still loves them.
The parent crying after everyone has gone to sleep.
The young adult who has confused worldly success with spiritual security.
The longtime church member whose heart has grown cold.
The person with a scandalous past who believes that redemption belongs to everyone except them.
They need to know that Jesus still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
That His grace is sufficient to save.
That His Word is trustworthy.
That holiness matters.
That forgiveness is real.
That transformation is possible through Him.
And that no human being is beyond the reach of Christ simply because the world has already written them off.
Because the mission is not to make the Gospel a luxury.
The mission is to help more people know the Savior.
Not simply to increase a number on a screen, but because someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances may be silently struggling with the very things Jesus has confronted here.
Someone may be comparing their life with everyone else's.
Someone may have spent years serving God and grown bitter.
Someone may be convinced that their past disqualifies them from receiving mercy.
Someone may need to hear that being last in the world's eyes does not make them worthless before God.

Return to Matthew 19:16–30 and Matthew 20:1–28. Read the passages in their full context. Test these reflections against Scripture. Let God's Word, not merely the emotions of this moment, shape your understanding.
You do not need to have every question answered before you begin seeking Jesus.
And you do not need to pretend your life is perfect before you open His Word.
Because we are not gathering around the idea that we are better than everyone else.
We are gathering around the truth that Jesus Christ is the Savior we all desperately need.
And perhaps that is the most important thing to remember about the first and the last.
At the end of the day, the greatest blessing was never merely the denarius.
The workers had been invited into the vineyard.
And for us, the greater wonder is not that we might someday stand ahead of someone else.
It is that through Jesus Christ, sinners who could never save themselves may be forgiven, reconciled to God, and welcomed into His Kingdom.
That is worth more than recognition.
More than status.
More than the applause of a thousand people.
So stop asking whether you are ahead of everyone else.
Ask whether you are following Jesus.
Stop looking at another person's grace as though it diminishes your own.
Look again at the cross.
And if you have been standing outside, convinced that your hour has passed, hear the Gospel's invitation today.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Not because you deserve salvation.
But because He is merciful, mighty to save, and worthy of your trust.
The greatest tragedy is not arriving last. It is standing so close to grace that you can see others receiving it, while pride keeps your own heart from rejoicing in the Savior.
